stories.headline: Amul and Mother Dairy raise milk prices as inflation nears 6%
stories.question: Why are milk prices rising again, and is inflation really hitting 6%?
stories.dek: Dairies say they pay more for milk, feed and packaging, so pouch milk costs ₹2–4 more a litre. Economists expect October inflation near 6%, partly because October 2025's base was so low.

so_far.text: Milk prices last rose on 14 May 2026, when Amul and Mother Dairy added ₹2 a litre. Amul blamed cattle feed, packaging film, fuel and food inflation made worse by the West Asia conflict. Mother Dairy cited about 6% higher prices paid to farmers. In October 2026 the RBI raised its repo rate to 5.5%. On 1 November, Karnataka's Nandini raised milk prices by ₹8–12 a litre.

what_happened.text: From 12 November 2026, days before Chhath Puja, Amul and Mother Dairy charge more for pouch milk. Amul Gold rose ₹4 a litre (about 5.5%) and Amul Taaza ₹2 (about 3.3%). GCMMF, which sells Amul, cited higher costs of milk, cattle feed, packaging and processing. In Delhi-NCR, Mother Dairy full cream milk went from ₹72 to ₹76 a litre, toned from ₹60 to ₹62 and cow milk from ₹62 to ₹65. Sources quoted by PTI said Mother Dairy is partly passing on higher farmer prices. October inflation data is due on 12 November; a Mint poll of 15 economists expects 6%.

steps.text: Dairies are paying farmers more for raw milk, and cattle feed, packaging and processing also cost more.
Dairies say they are passing these costs on to buyers; Nandini sent ₹7 of its ₹8–12 rise to farmers.
Food and beverages are 36.75% of the CPI basket, so milk and food rises lift overall inflation.
October 2025 inflation was a record-low 0.25%, so October 2026's yearly comparison starts from a low base.
At 6%, inflation would touch the RBI's upper limit, adding pressure for another rate rise in December.

history.text: India's milk story starts with farmers, not companies. On 14 December 1946, dairy farmers in Gujarat's Kaira district formed the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union, led by Tribhuvandas Patel. Their aim was to end exploitation by traders and to break the Polson company's monopoly. In 1949 Verghese Kurien joined the union, and in 1955 it adopted the Amul brand. In 1964-65 the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) was set up to copy the Kaira cooperative model across India, so one district's idea became a national plan. In 1970 Operation Flood, also called the White Revolution, was launched under Kurien. It made India the world's largest milk producer. In 1973 GCMMF was set up as the marketing body for Gujarat's district milk unions and took over the Amul brand. GCMMF is the body behind the November 2026 Amul hike. The recent turning points are about prices. In October 2025, inflation fell to a record low of 0.25%, helped by falling food prices and GST cuts. That low level became the base that October 2026 is measured against. In May 2026 Amul and Mother Dairy raised milk by ₹2 a litre. In November 2026 Nandini, then Amul and Mother Dairy, raised prices again.

lesson.concept: How the base effect shapes yearly inflation
lesson.big_idea: India's inflation figure compares prices with the same month a year earlier. That earlier level is the base. If the base was unusually low, even ordinary rises now look large.

steps.title: Inflation is a yearly comparison
steps.text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is like a price tag on a fixed basket of things households buy. Inflation is how much that tag changed from the same month a year earlier.

steps.title: The base is last year's level
steps.text: The month you compare against is the base. If prices were flat or falling then, the base is low. Any normal rise a year later then shows up as a bigger percentage.

steps.title: October 2025 was very low
steps.text: In October 2025, inflation was a record-low 0.25%, after falling food prices and GST cuts. So October 2026 is measured against a cheap starting point.

steps.title: Real rises add on top
steps.text: The base explains only part. Real price hikes, like milk, push the index up further. Economists expect October 2026 at 6%, the RBI's upper tolerance limit.

example.setup: Imagine a family's monthly groceries cost ₹10,000 in October of Year 1. Prices stayed flat, so they still cost ₹10,000 in October of Year 2.

lines.label: The base
lines.note: A flat year, like October 2025's very low inflation

lines.label: This October
lines.note: Prices rose through the year

lines.label: Yearly inflation
lines.note: The rise divided by the base

lines.label: If base were normal
lines.note: Same ₹10,600 this October, smaller rise

lines.label: The difference
lines.note: The low base roughly doubles the reading

example.result: The family pays ₹10,600 either way. But because the year before was flat, measured inflation is 6% instead of about 2.9%. The base changes the headline number, not the bill the family pays.

apply.text: October 2025 inflation was a record-low 0.25%, so October 2026 starts from a low base. That helps explain why economists polled by Mint expect 6%, up from 5.5% in September. Icra's Aditi Nayar links part of the rise to this base. The milk hikes from 12 November are real rises on top, and fall in November's data.

practice.q: Your basket cost ₹20,000 last October, after a flat year. This October it costs ₹21,000. What is inflation? What if last October's base had been ₹20,500?
practice.answer: Rise: ₹21,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,000. ₹1,000 ÷ ₹20,000 = 5%. With a ₹20,500 base: rise = ₹500. ₹500 ÷ ₹20,500 ≈ 2.4%. Same price this October, but the lower base gives the higher rate.

stories.headline: Iran says its uranium stays home as oil markets bet on peace
stories.question: Is the Iran war winding down if Tehran still refuses to hand over its uranium?
stories.dek: Not cleanly. Trump's talk of an end pushed oil below $90. But on 11 November Iran's security chief said enriched material stays in Iran, and that stockpile is central to any deal.

so_far.text: After the ceasefire collapsed on 8 July 2026, the war spread further. In September, Houthi attacks began a crisis at the Bab al-Mandab strait. On 20 October, Iran's security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir that no enriched material would leave Iran. Then Donald Trump met Qatar's prime minister. Afterwards he said he was not considering attacking Iran 'at this point' and that the war could end 'fairly soon'. Brent crude fell 17% that week, its worst week since the 2020 Covid lockdowns.

what_happened.text: On 11 November, Reuters reported that Iran's security chief said Iran will not let enriched nuclear material leave the country. Oil rose about 1% that day, a partial rebound after a steep slide. On 10 November, Brent crude had dipped to $89.70 a barrel, its first move below $90 since August. Also on 10 November, a projectile hit the tanker MT Fujairah Energy in the Persian Gulf. Four crew were hurt, including one of six Indian seafarers aboard. New data showed OPEC+ pumped 97% of its pre-war output in October.

steps.text: Oil prices carry a fear premium: buyers pay extra when they think war may cut supply.
Trump's talk of an end shrank that fear, so Brent fell 17% in a week and slipped below $90.
Supply also came back: OPEC+ pumped 97% of pre-war output in October, helped by pipelines that bypass Hormuz.
But a lasting deal needs an answer on Iran's enriched uranium, and the IAEA cannot verify where it is.
Iran's refusal to send it abroad makes a quick deal look harder, so some fear returned and oil rose about 1%.

history.text: The fight over Iran's uranium started long before this war. In 2015 Iran and world powers signed the JCPOA, a deal that limited Iran's nuclear programme. In 2018 Trump pulled the US out, brought sanctions back and began 'maximum pressure'. Trust between the two sides never recovered. In June 2025, during the Twelve-Day War, Israel and the US struck Iranian nuclear sites. On 12 June 2025 the IAEA, the UN's nuclear watchdog, found Iran non-compliant. UN sanctions came back through 'snapback' in September 2025. By February 2026 the IAEA could not verify Iran's enriched-uranium stockpile, so nobody outside Iran knew where it was. On 28 February 2026 the US and Israel struck Iran and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Mojtaba Khamenei became leader. Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, causing a global fuel crisis. A ceasefire began on 8 April. Talks in Islamabad failed, and the US imposed a naval blockade. In May, sources said Mojtaba Khamenei ordered the stockpile to stay in Iran. The US reportedly tied its removal to releasing about $20 billion in frozen funds. A memorandum on 17 June ended the blockades. Then the ceasefire collapsed on 8 July after Iran attacked ships. That is why, as of 11 November 2026, the uranium is still the hardest question.

lesson.concept: How a war 'fear premium' moves oil prices
lesson.big_idea: An oil price has two parts: a base price set by supply and demand, plus a 'fear premium' for the risk that war cuts supply. News that changes fear moves the premium fastest.

steps.title: Start with supply and demand
steps.text: Without a war, oil settles at the price where barrels pumped match barrels buyers want. Call this the base price. More supply, with the same demand, pushes the base price down.

steps.title: Add the fear premium
steps.text: When war threatens a route like the Strait of Hormuz, buyers pay extra to secure oil before it might vanish. That extra amount, above the base price, is the fear premium.

steps.title: Fear moves faster than supply
steps.text: Pumping more oil takes weeks. Fear can change with one speech. After Trump said the war could end 'fairly soon', Brent fell 17% in one week.

steps.title: More barrels lower the base
steps.text: In October OPEC+ pumped 97% of its pre-war output, partly through pipelines that avoid Hormuz. That pulls the base price down, separately from fear.

steps.title: Hard words add fear back
steps.text: If one side refuses a key deal term, quick peace looks less likely. Some premium returns and the price ticks up, as it did on 11 November.

example.setup: Imagine a barrel of oil whose base price, from supply and demand alone, is $70. Assume war fear adds $40 on top. All numbers here are made up.

lines.label: Price at peak fear
lines.note: Buyers pay extra in case supply stops.

lines.label: Peace talk halves fear
lines.note: A leader says the war may end soon.

lines.label: New price
lines.note: A $20 drop, about 18% of $110, with no change in barrels.

lines.label: Hard words return
lines.note: About a 1% rise, like 11 November.

lines.label: Supply recovers
lines.note: More barrels lower the base even while fear stays.

example.result: Most of the big swing came from fear, not barrels. That is why words from Trump or Iran move oil quickly, while extra pumping works more slowly in the background.

apply.text: So on 10 November, Trump's talk of peace had shrunk the fear premium, and Brent slipped to $89.70. On 11 November, Iran's security chief said enriched material will not leave Iran. That made a quick deal look harder, so some fear returned and oil rose about 1%. Meanwhile OPEC+, at 97% of pre-war output, keeps pulling the base price down.

practice.q: The base price is $70 and the fear premium is $20, so oil costs $90. A big tanker attack doubles the premium. What is the new price, and how big is the rise?
practice.answer: The premium doubles: $20 × 2 = $40. New price: $70 + $40 = $110. Rise: $110 − $90 = $20. As a share: $20 ÷ $90 ≈ 22%. The base did not change; only fear did.

stories.headline: Abu Dhabi talks end with prisoner deal but no peace breakthrough
stories.question: Abu Dhabi talks ended without a breakthrough, so what comes next for Ukraine?
stories.dek: The talks ended on 11 November with a large prisoner exchange agreed but no deal to end the war. Next, US envoys head to Moscow, and the Kremlin wants European security on the table.

so_far.text: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022. The US has since mediated talks between the two sides. In February 2026, a round in Abu Dhabi produced a swap of 314 prisoners, 157 from each side, but left territory unresolved. The third round of US-mediated talks began in Abu Dhabi on 10 November 2026. It focused on humanitarian impact, prisoners of war and security guarantees. Before it started, the US and Ukraine met France, Germany, Italy, the UK, the European Commission and NATO.

what_happened.text: The Abu Dhabi talks ended on 11 November 2026 without a breakthrough on ending the war. Russia and Ukraine agreed a large prisoner exchange, AP and Al Jazeera reported, but no number or date has been given. The BBC says the talks centred on Europe's post-war security framework. Reuters reported that both sides said some progress was made, while the US cited a lack of trust. As the round ended, Trump's envoys said they would go to Moscow. The BBC reports US envoys are due to meet Putin and Zelensky on 12 November.

steps.text: A prisoner swap is small and checkable, so each side can test the other's word at little risk.
Land is different: Russia claims four Ukrainian regions as annexed and occupies roughly 20 per cent of Ukraine.
Land cannot be handed over in small steps that can be undone, so it needs trust; the US cited a lack of it.
The Kremlin also wants talks on European security structures, which pulls Europe in; the US urged Russia to include Europe.
So the next move leaves the table: US envoys head to Moscow and are due to meet Putin and Zelensky.

history.text:
The roots go back to 2014. President Yanukovych fled during protests. Russia then seized and annexed Crimea, and Russia-backed separatists began a war in Donbas, in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. This started the fight over land that still blocks peace.

In 2014 and 2015 the Minsk agreements aimed at a ceasefire in Donbas. They largely froze the front lines, left the status of rebel areas unresolved, and ultimately failed. They showed how a pause in fighting can freeze a dispute without settling it.

On 24 February 2022 Putin announced a full-scale invasion. Ukraine pushed Russian forces back from Kyiv, Russia withdrew from the capital region in March, and Ukraine retook Kherson by November. Late in 2022 Russia moved to annex the occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, an act described as illegal. Once Russia claimed these regions as its own, land became far harder to bargain over.

Talks slowly returned. In May 2025 delegations met in Istanbul, the first direct talks since early 2022, producing the war's largest prisoner swap. On 15 August 2025 Trump and Putin met in Alaska, with no clear progress. In November 2025 Ukraine rejected a 28-point US-Russia draft; a revised 20-point plan followed in December. In February 2026 an Abu Dhabi round swapped 314 prisoners but left territory unresolved. A three-day ceasefire in May 2026 quickly unravelled. Russia still occupies roughly 20 per cent of Ukraine.

lesson.concept: How small deals build trust in peace talks
lesson.big_idea: Enemies who don't trust each other start with small deals they can check step by step, like prisoner swaps. Big deals that can't be undone, like borders, wait until trust exists.

steps.title: Talks start from distrust
steps.text: At war, each side assumes the other may cheat. A promise is only worth something if you can see it kept. As the Abu Dhabi round ended, the US cited exactly this: a lack of trust.

steps.title: Pick deals you can check
steps.text: A confidence-building measure is a small deal both sides can verify. A prisoner swap fits well: people cross at an agreed point, and each side can count who arrives.

steps.title: Split the deal into batches
steps.text: Doing a swap in batches limits the risk. If one side cheats on a batch, the other loses only that batch and stops. Each completed batch is proof that promises are kept.

steps.title: Big deals cannot be split
steps.text: Land and security arrangements are hard to hand over in small pieces that can be undone. Giving up a region is one large, final move, so it needs much more trust first.

steps.title: Small deals alone don't end wars
steps.text: Kept promises make the next deal easier, but they are not peace. Russia and Ukraine swapped prisoners in May 2025 and February 2026, and the war went on.

example.setup: Imagine two sides agree to swap 600 prisoners each, done in three equal batches on the same day at one border crossing.

lines.label: Size of each batch
lines.note: Each batch is one third of the deal.

lines.label: Batch 1
lines.calc: 200 cross each way; both sides count
lines.note: Each side checks the other kept its word.

lines.label: If one side cheats
lines.note: It simply stops sending, so its loss is capped.

lines.label: After batch 3
lines.note: Three promises made, three checked.

lines.label: Now try land
lines.calc: Hand over one region: cannot split, cannot undo
lines.note: No batches, so no way to test the other side first.

example.result: Splitting a swap cuts the worst-case loss to one third, so even distrustful enemies can agree to it. Land cannot be split that way, which is why swaps happen while territory stalls.

apply.text: This is what happened in Abu Dhabi. In February 2026 the sides swapped 314 prisoners, 157 each, but left territory unresolved. On 11 November they agreed another large exchange, yet made no breakthrough on ending the war. The US cited a lack of trust, and the Kremlin added a bigger demand: talks on European security structures.

practice.q: Suppose the sides agree to swap 1,200 prisoners each in four equal batches. If one side cheats on the first batch, what is the most the honest side can lose?
practice.answer: Batch size: 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 per side. In the first batch, the honest side sends 300. If the other side cheats, the honest side stops, so its other 900 stay put. Worst-case loss: 300, one quarter of the deal, instead of all 1,200.

so_far.text: COP31, the yearly UN climate summit, opened on 9 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye. Countries arrived with different goals. The EU wants a Brazil-led roadmap away from fossil fuels written into the summit's main decision. But it is reportedly bringing no new adaptation money. China wants talks on trade rules that restrict clean-technology equipment, and its top leaders are not expected. Türkiye is promoting a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of final energy use to 35% by 2035; Australia has signed up. India wants a formal decision launching a Climate Finance Work Programme.

what_happened.text: The United States has sent no official delegation to COP31 in Antalya, the second year in a row. The US State Department told NPR by email that it will not send one, as reported on 9 November 2026. A White House official said the summit 'rejects reality' by ignoring that 'extremist climate policies are destroying countries'. The official said the administration is pursuing an 'energy dominance' agenda. Instead, more than 120 US state and local leaders, led by New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, are expected to attend without the federal government. Several key EU leaders are also skipping the World Leaders' Summit on 11–12 November.

steps.text: COP decisions need consensus among the countries in the room, so a country with no delegation cannot block any text.
But the US also brings nothing: the White House rejects the summit and backs an 'energy dominance' agenda instead.
The EU is reportedly arriving with no new adaptation money either, so little new finance is expected overall.
India links action to money: it opposes new top-down cut targets and wants finance treated as a rich-country obligation.
So progress shifts to voluntary pledges, like Türkiye's '35 by 35', that countries join one at a time.

history.text: The story starts in May 1992. At the Rio Earth Summit, countries adopted the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It took effect on 21 March 1994. Its members meet every year at a summit called a COP. In December 1997 the Kyoto Protocol bound rich countries to cut emissions; it took effect in 2005. That split the world into countries with a duty to cut and countries without one. In 2009 the Copenhagen Accord set a 2°C goal. It also promised developing countries $100 billion a year by 2020. That put a money promise from rich to poorer countries at the centre of the talks. The Paris Agreement of 2015 aimed to hold warming well below 2°C, preferably 1.5°C. It took effect for the US in November 2016. Then US policy began to swing with each president. Trump announced a US exit from Paris on 1 June 2017; it took effect on 4 November 2020. Biden rejoined, formally returning on 19 February 2021. On 20 January 2025 Trump signed an order to withdraw a second time. COP31 is now the second summit in a row with no official US delegation.

lesson.concept: How a UN climate summit reaches a deal
lesson.big_idea: At a COP, a decision passes only if no country in the room objects. So an absent country cannot block a deal, but it adds no money or pledges to make the deal work.

steps.title: Countries meet once a year
steps.text: In 1992 countries adopted a UN climate treaty, the UNFCCC. Its members meet every year at a summit called a COP, short for Conference of the Parties. COP31 opened on 9 November 2026 in Antalya.

steps.title: No vote, only consensus
steps.text: COPs do not decide by majority vote. A decision is adopted when no country in the room formally objects. That gives every delegation present a kind of veto over the wording.

steps.title: Absent means no veto
steps.text: A country with no delegation cannot object. That can make agreeing on words easier. But that country also promises nothing: no money, no new cuts, no name on voluntary pledges.

steps.title: Words and money are separate
steps.text: A decision can set a goal, but each country decides what it actually pays or pledges. Voluntary pledges, like Türkiye's '35 by 35' electricity goal, are joined one country at a time.

example.setup: Imagine 10 countries meet to agree a climate fund with a goal of ₹100 crore a year. One large country stays home. The other nine each offer ₹5 crore.

lines.label: The draft text
lines.note: The chair puts the proposed decision to the room.

lines.label: Who can object?
lines.note: Consensus counts only countries in the room.

lines.label: Deal adopted
lines.note: Nobody opposed is present to block it.

lines.label: Money offered
lines.note: Each present country pledges its own share (assume).

lines.label: The gap
lines.note: The absent country adds nothing.

example.result: The deal passed easily, yet it is funded at less than half its goal. Skipping a summit removes a possible veto, but it also removes that country's money.

apply.text: With no official delegation, the US cannot object to any COP31 text. But it brings nothing either: a White House official calls the summit out of touch and backs 'energy dominance'. With the EU also bringing no new adaptation money, the real gap looks like our example: $305 billion a year needed by 2035, against $28.2–31.7 billion in 2024.

practice.q: Same 10 countries. This time the large country attends, does not object, and pledges ₹30 crore. The other nine still give ₹5 crore each. What is the gap?
practice.answer: Nine countries give 9 × ₹5 crore = ₹45 crore. Add the large country's ₹30 crore: ₹45 crore + ₹30 crore = ₹75 crore. Gap: ₹100 crore − ₹75 crore = ₹25 crore. Attending gave it a chance to object, but its money cut the gap from ₹55 crore to ₹25 crore.

scenes.speak: 1997 में Kyoto Protocol ने अमीर देशों को emissions cut करने के लिए बाँधा। 2009 में Copenhagen Accord ने 2 degree का goal रखा, और गरीब देशों से 2020 तक हर साल 100 billion dollar का वादा किया। इससे पैसा centre में आ गया। 2015 में Paris Agreement का target था 2 degree से काफ़ी नीचे, हो सके तो 1 point 5।

January 2025 mein Trump ne doosri baar exit ka order diya. Aur ab, lagaataar doosra summit bina US team ke.

China clean technology par trade curbs pe baat chahta hai, aur uske top leaders ke aane ki ummeed nahi hai.

scenes.say: Toh US ka na hona kyun matter karta hai? Pehle rules dekhiye. COP ke decisions ke liye room mein maujood deshon ki consensus chahiye. Isliye jis desh ka delegation hi nahi, woh kisi text ko block nahi kar sakta. Lekin woh kuch laata bhi nahi. White House iski jagah energy dominance ke saath khada hai.

India emissions cut karne ke naye top-down targets ke khilaaf hai, aur chahta hai ki finance ko amir deshon ki zimmedari maana jaaye. Isliye progress voluntary pledges ki taraf shift hoti hai, jinmein desh ek-ek karke judte hain.
scenes.speak: European Union भी कोई नया adaptation पैसा नहीं ला रहा, तो नए finance की उम्मीद कम है। India emissions cut करने के नए top-down targets के खिलाफ़ है, और चाहता है कि finance को अमीर देशों की ज़िम्मेदारी माना जाए। इसलिए progress voluntary pledges की तरफ़ shift होती है, जिनमें देश एक-एक करके जुड़ते हैं।

scenes.say: Ab woh ek idea jo seekhna hai: UN climate summit mein deal kaise banti hai? Yahan majority vote nahi hota. Decision tabhi pass hota hai jab room mein koi bhi desh formally objection na kare. Matlab wahan maujood har delegation ke paas ek tarah ka veto hai.
scenes.show: Consensus: no objection in the room
scenes.speak: अब वो एक idea जो सीखना है: UN climate summit में deal कैसे बनती है? यहाँ majority vote नहीं होता। Decision तभी pass होता है जब room में कोई भी देश formally objection ना करे। मतलब वहाँ मौजूद हर delegation के पास एक तरह का veto है।

scenes.say: Jis desh ka delegation hi nahi, woh objection nahi kar sakta. Isse words par agree karna aasaan ho sakta hai. Lekin words aur paisa alag cheezein hain. Decision ek goal set kar sakta hai, par kaun kitna dega, yeh har desh khud tay karta hai, aur voluntary pledges mein ek-ek karke judta hai.
scenes.speak: जिस देश का delegation ही नहीं, वो objection नहीं कर सकता। इससे words पर agree करना आसान हो सकता है। लेकिन words और पैसा अलग चीज़ें हैं। Decision एक goal set कर सकता है, पर कौन कितना देगा, यह हर देश खुद तय करता है, और voluntary pledges में एक-एक करके जुड़ता है।

scenes.say: Chaliye try karte hain. Maan lijiye 10 desh ek climate fund par agree karte hain. Goal hai har saal 100 crore rupaye. Ek bada desh ghar par reh jaata hai. Objection sirf wahan maujood 9 desh kar sakte hain. Koi nahi karta, toh deal adopt ho jaati hai.
scenes.speak: चलिए try करते हैं। मान लीजिए 10 देश एक climate fund पर agree करते हैं। Goal है हर साल 100 करोड़ रुपये। एक बड़ा देश घर पर रह जाता है। Objection सिर्फ़ वहाँ मौजूद 9 देश कर सकते हैं। कोई नहीं करता, तो deal adopt हो जाती है।

scenes.say: Ab paisa. 9 mein se har desh 5 crore rupaye offer karta hai. 9 guna 5, yaani 45 crore. Ise 100 crore ke goal se ghataiye, toh gap bacha 55 crore. Deal aasaani se pass ho gayi, lekin funding goal ke aadhe se bhi kam hai.
scenes.speak: अब पैसा। 9 में से हर देश 5 करोड़ रुपये offer करता है। 9 गुना 5, यानी 45 करोड़। इसे 100 करोड़ के goal से घटाइए, तो gap बचा 55 करोड़। Deal आसानी से pass हो गई, लेकिन funding goal के आधे से भी कम है।

scenes.say: Sides kya kehti hain? White House ke ek official kehte hain ki summit reality ko reject karta hai. India kehta hai ki Article 9 point 1 ke tahat climate finance amir deshon ki obligation hai. European Union chahta hai ki fossil fuel roadmap main decision mein ho.
scenes.speak: Sides क्या कहती हैं? White House के एक official कहते हैं कि summit reality को reject करता है। India कहता है कि Article 9 point 1 के तहत climate finance अमीर देशों की obligation है। European Union चाहता है कि fossil fuel roadmap main decision में हो।

views.view: Summit 'rejects reality'; US pursues energy dominance
Climate finance is a rich-country obligation under Article 9.1
Put the fossil fuel roadmap in the main decision

scenes.say: India mein aapke liye iska kya matlab hai? Aapke bills ya loan payments par direct asar chhota hai. Bada asar paise par hai. India chahta hai predictable, zyaadatar public, aur sasta climate finance. Naya paisa kam aa raha hai, toh garmi aur baadh se nipatne ke funds ke jaldi badhne ki ummeed kam hai.
scenes.show: Small direct effect; finance is key
scenes.speak: India में आपके लिए इसका क्या मतलब है? आपके bills या loan payments पर direct असर छोटा है। बड़ा असर पैसे पर है। India चाहता है predictable, ज़्यादातर public, और सस्ता climate finance। नया पैसा कम आ रहा है, तो गर्मी और बाढ़ से निपटने के funds के जल्दी बढ़ने की उम्मीद कम है।

scenes.say: Ek aam myth: America ke bina koi climate deal ho hi nahi sakti. Galat. Decisions wahan maujood desh lete hain, isliye gair-haazir US block nahi kar sakta. Bilkul hamare example ki tarah, asli nuksaan paise ka hai, aur adaptation gap bada hi rehta hai.
scenes.speak: एक आम myth: America के बिना कोई climate deal हो ही नहीं सकती। गलत। Decisions वहाँ मौजूद देश लेते हैं, इसलिए गैर-हाज़िर US block नहीं कर सकता। बिल्कुल हमारे example की तरह, असली नुकसान पैसे का है, और adaptation gap बड़ा ही रहता है।

scenes.say: Aage kya? World Leaders Summit 12 November ko khatam hota hai, aur kai bade European leaders usmein nahi hain. Uske baad dekhiye ki finance programme aur fossil fuel roadmap COP31 ke final text mein aate hain ya nahi. Ek baat ab bhi pata nahi: UN climate treaty se kisi bhi US exit ka exact status.
scenes.speak: आगे क्या? World Leaders Summit 12 November को खत्म होता है, और कई बड़े European leaders उसमें नहीं हैं। उसके बाद देखिए कि finance programme और fossil fuel roadmap COP31 के final text में आते हैं या नहीं। एक बात अब भी पता नहीं: UN climate treaty से किसी भी US exit का exact status।

scenes.say: Teen baatein yaad rakhiye. COP deals ke liye maujood deshon ki consensus chahiye, isliye gair-haazir desh block nahi kar sakte, par paisa bhi nahi jodte. US ne lagaataar doosre saal COP31 skip kiya, aur finance patla hi hai. Aur dekhiye ki finance aur fossil fuel roadmap COP31 ke final decisions mein jagah banate hain ya nahi.
scenes.speak: तीन बातें याद रखिए। COP deals के लिए मौजूद देशों की consensus चाहिए, इसलिए गैर-हाज़िर देश block नहीं कर सकते, पर पैसा भी नहीं जोड़ते। US ने लगातार दूसरे साल COP31 skip किया, और finance पतला ही है। और देखिए कि finance और fossil fuel roadmap COP31 के final decisions में जगह बनाते हैं या नहीं।

stories.headline: India plans to cut visa types from 13 to nine
stories.question: What will India's simpler visa rules change for tourists, business visitors and patients?
stories.dek: Reports say the Home Ministry plans nine visa categories instead of 13 and forms about 70% shorter, with security checks unchanged. Fewer boxes should mean fewer errors, but no start date is set.

so_far.text: A visa is a country's permission to enter for a set purpose, such as tourism, business or medical treatment. Indian officials follow a rulebook called the Visa Manual, 2019. Reports say it sorts visas into 13 main categories and 49 sub-categories. The Home Ministry has been reviewing this manual, including at a high-level meeting in August. Reports say it picked three areas to fix: fewer categories, merged sub-categories and simpler forms.

what_happened.text: On 5 November 2026 Business Today, citing sources, reported the Home Ministry's plan. Main visa categories would fall from 13 to nine, to align with global norms. Sub-categories would be merged from 49 to 23. About 70% of entry fields in application forms would go, targeting overlapping and repeated ones. Core security and background checks stay intact. On 11 November 2026 The Hindu and NDTV reported the same simplification; NDTV said it covers tourism, business and medical visas. No start date has been given.

steps.text: India's visa rulebook, the Visa Manual, 2019, sorts visitors into 13 main categories and 49 sub-categories.
Reports say the application forms carry overlapping, repetitive and redundant boxes that ask for the same details again.
Every extra choice or box is a chance for an applicant or an official to make an error.
Merging categories and cutting about 70% of boxes removes many of those chances, so fewer forms need correcting.
Security does not loosen, because the background checks themselves are kept intact; only the paperwork shrinks.

history.text: India's modern visa story starts on 27 November 2014. That day an online visa, then called the Electronic Travel Authorisation, went live for citizens of more than 40 countries. From then, visitors from those countries could apply online. In April 2015 it was renamed the e-Tourist Visa, and on 1 May 2015 it opened to 31 more countries. Early uptake was modest: the Observer Research Foundation reported that only 8.81% of foreign travellers used it between December 2014 and February 2017. On 30 November 2016 the government approved further liberalisation, simplification and rationalisation of the visa regime. On 1 April 2017 the scheme became the e-Visa, split into e-Tourist, e-Business and e-Medical types. Then COVID-19 struck. In March 2020 business and medical e-visas were suspended. An order of 30 March 2021 restored e-Business, e-Medical, e-Medical Attendant and e-Conference visas, while tourist e-visas stayed suspended. The rules officials follow are gathered in the Visa Manual, 2019. That manual is what the Home Ministry has reviewed, and the November 2026 reports say its categories and forms will be cut.

lesson.concept: Why fewer visa boxes mean fewer mistakes
lesson.big_idea: Every category you must choose and every box you must fill is a chance to get something wrong. Remove repeated choices and boxes, and mistakes fall, even if the checks stay the same.

steps.title: A visa matches a purpose
steps.text: A visa is permission to enter a country for a stated purpose. Each purpose, such as tourism, business or medical treatment, is a category with its own rules.

steps.title: Categories split into sub-categories
steps.text: Each main category splits into narrower sub-categories, each with its own conditions. Reports say India has 13 main categories and 49 sub-categories. Picking the wrong one can mean delay or rejection.

steps.title: Every box is a chance to slip
steps.text: A form box is one question. If each box carries a small chance of a typo or wrong answer, more boxes mean more expected mistakes. Repeated boxes add risk but no new information.

steps.title: Cut boxes, keep the checks
steps.text: Removing repeated boxes lowers the expected number of mistakes. The background checks, which look at who you are, are a separate step and can stay the same. Reports say India keeps them intact.

example.setup: Imagine one batch of 1,000 visa applications for India. Each form has 100 boxes. Assume one box in every 200 is filled in wrongly.

lines.note: Every applicant fills every box.

lines.label: Mistakes after
lines.note: Same people, same error rate.

lines.label: Mistakes avoided
lines.note: The applicant and processing errors the cut aims to reduce.

example.result: Cutting 70% of the boxes cuts expected mistakes by 70% too, from 500 to 150 in the batch, without changing who gets checked or how.

apply.text: So when the Home Ministry plans to merge 49 sub-categories into 23 and remove about 70% of form boxes, it is cutting the number of chances to slip, as in our example. Fewer forms should go back for correction, while core security checks stay intact. The real gain depends on rules not yet published.

practice.q: Say 2,000 people apply, each form has 50 boxes, and one box in 100 is filled wrongly. How many mistakes are avoided after a 70% cut?
practice.answer: Before: 2,000 × 50 = 1,00,000 boxes; ÷ 100 = 1,000 mistakes. After: 70% of 50 is 35, so 15 boxes remain. 2,000 × 15 = 30,000 boxes; ÷ 100 = 300 mistakes. Avoided: 1,000 − 300 = 700.

stories.headline: Fake court orders got 129 betting websites blocked in India
stories.question: How did fake court orders lead India to take down websites?
stories.dek: India's telecoms department told internet providers to block 129 betting sites, citing two High Court orders that Reuters found were forged. Clear red flags were missed, exposing a weak link in India's blocking system.

so_far.text: In India, courts and the government can order websites blocked. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) passes court orders to internet providers as 'blocking directions', and the providers cut access. Reuters calls this content-removal system one of the world's strictest. It has a safeguard. DoT letters forwarding Delhi High Court blocking orders carry a QR code, so providers can re-check the order on the court's portal. The system is also contested. In September 2025 the Karnataka High Court upheld the government's Sahyog portal. X Corp says that portal skips the safeguards of Section 69A of the IT Act.

what_happened.text: On 11 November 2026 Reuters reported that India had ordered internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites this year. The basis was two High Court orders that Reuters found to be fake. The DoT issued the blocking directions on 21 July and 2 September 2026. Reuters found neither attached order in the courts' online records. The Rajasthan order covered 34 sites and the Allahabad order covered 95. Prompted by Reuters, the Allahabad High Court found its order fake and filed a police complaint on 6 November. Police are investigating unknown persons for forgery and cheating. No arrests have been made.

steps.text: A court order to block sites goes to the DoT, which turns it into a blocking direction for internet providers.
Providers act on DoT directions, so whatever order the DoT attaches decides which sites go dark.
The forged orders looked official, with blue court seals bearing India's national emblem.
Simple checks would have exposed them: neither was in court records, one QR code misled, one email bounced.
The DoT issued the directions anyway, for reasons it has not explained, and 129 sites were blocked.

history.text:
This story starts with a long argument over who may block websites, and with what checks. In 2015 the Supreme Court's Shreya Singhal ruling became India's key free-speech precedent on blocking. The Karnataka High Court later said the system that ruling addressed has been replaced by a newer framework.

Safeguards were then built into the paperwork. By March 2025, DoT letters forwarding Delhi High Court blocking orders carried a QR code, so internet providers could re-check each order on the court's portal. Checking an order now depended on whoever received it actually doing so.

New routes brought new fights. On 24 September 2025 the Karnataka High Court dismissed X Corp's challenge to the Sahyog portal, ruling that the portal only transmits notices. X had argued that Sahyog is a parallel blocking route without the safeguards of Section 69A of the IT Act. X appealed in November 2025.

In 2026 the checks were tested by forgery. On 21 July and 2 September the DoT issued blocking directions attaching purported High Court orders that carried clear red flags. In early November, X told an Indian court that police directives sent to two free-speech groups were fake. On 6 November the Allahabad High Court filed a police complaint. On 11 November Reuters published its findings.

for_you.text: The 129 were illegal betting sites, so most readers will not miss them. The bigger point is trust in the system: two forged orders passed through the DoT despite clear red flags. lesson.concept: How a court order becomes a website block
lesson.big_idea: A website block in India is a relay: a court decides, the DoT passes the order on, and internet providers cut access. Each hand-off trusts the last, so checking the first paper matters most.

steps.title: Someone with power decides
steps.text: It starts with an order, for example from a High Court, naming websites to block. A genuine court order sits in that court's online records, so anyone can look it up.

steps.title: The DoT passes it on
steps.text: The Department of Telecommunications turns the order into a 'blocking direction'. It sends this to internet providers, with the court order attached.

steps.title: Providers cut access
steps.text: Internet providers, the firms that connect your phone or broadband, then stop users reaching the listed sites. They act because the direction comes from the government.

steps.title: Checking is the gatekeeper
steps.text: Each runner trusts the one before, so the check must happen early. DoT letters forwarding Delhi High Court orders carry a QR code, a scannable square, so providers can re-check the order on the court's portal.

steps.title: A forgery runs the whole relay
steps.text: If nobody checks the court records, the QR code or the sender, a fake order travels exactly like a real one. Every provider then blocks every listed site.

example.setup: Imagine an official receives an emailed 'court order' to block 40 betting sites. It has a blue seal and a judge's signature. Assume five internet providers will act on it.

lines.label: Check 1: court records
lines.calc: Search the court website: no such order found
lines.note: A real order would be listed. The check should stop here.

lines.label: Check 2: QR code
lines.calc: Scan the code: it opens an unrelated page
lines.note: A genuine code leads to the order itself.

lines.label: Check 3: the sender
lines.calc: Reply to the email: the message bounces
lines.note: A real court office would answer.

lines.label: If all checks skipped
lines.note: Made-up numbers: each provider blocks every listed site.

lines.label: The result
lines.calc: Sites blocked; no court ordered it
lines.note: Each block works just like one based on a real order.

example.result: Any one check would have stopped the fake order at the first desk. Skip all three, and one forged paper becomes 200 separate blocks that work exactly like lawful ones.

apply.text: This is what Reuters found. The Allahabad order's QR code led to an unrelated page, and the signing judge's office said no such order was passed. The Rajasthan order came from an email that bounced. Neither order was in court records. Yet the DoT issued directions on 21 July and 2 September, and 129 sites were blocked.

practice.q: A letter says a High Court ordered 20 sites blocked. Its seal looks right. It is missing from the court's online records, and the judge's office denies it. Forward it?
practice.answer: No. Check 1, court records: fails, because it is not listed. Check 2, the judge's office: fails, because it denies the order. The seal proves nothing, since the forged orders had seals too. Stop and ask the court's registrar. If forwarded, 20 sites would be blocked by every provider with no court behind it.

check.q: Why were 129 sites blocked even though no court had ordered it?
options: Internet providers decided to block betting sites on their own
The DoT passed on forged orders, and the checks that could expose them did not stop it
The High Courts passed real orders and later withdrew them
check.why: The blocking relay trusts the paper at its start. Forged orders entered it, and the red flags did not stop the DoT directions.

Two forged High Court orders got 129 betting sites blocked despite clear red flags.

scenes.say: Ek court order sochiye, official seal aur judge ke signature ke saath. Likha hai: in websites ko block karo. Government use aage bhejti hai, aur internet providers maan lete hain. Bas ek problem hai. Yeh order kisi court ne likha hi nahi. Toh fake court orders se India mein websites band kaise ho gayi?
scenes.show: Fake court orders, real website blocks
scenes.speak: एक court order सोचिए, official seal और judge के signature के साथ। लिखा है: इन websites को block करो। Government उसे आगे भेजती है, और internet providers मान लेते हैं। बस एक problem है। यह order किसी court ने लिखा ही नहीं। तो fake court orders से India में websites बंद कैसे हो गईं?

scenes.say: 11 November 2026 ko news agency Reuters ne apni findings publish ki. India ne 2026 mein internet providers ko 129 illegal betting websites block karne ka order diya tha. Basis tha High Court ke 2 orders. Reuters ne paaya ki dono fake the.
scenes.show: 129 betting sites blocked on fake orders
scenes.speak: 11 November 2026 को news agency Reuters ने अपनी findings publish कीं। India ने 2026 में internet providers को 129 illegal betting websites block करने का order दिया था। Basis था High Court के 2 orders। Reuters ने पाया कि दोनों fake थे।

number.label: illegal betting websites blocked on two fake court orders

scenes.say: Department of Telecommunications, yaani telecom ka sarkari department, ne 2 blocking directions jaari kiye. Ek 21 July ko aaya, doosra 2 September ko. Har ek ke saath ek so-called High Court order laga tha. Reuters ne courts ke online records khangale. Dono mein se koi order wahan nahi tha.
scenes.speak: Department of Telecommunications, यानी telecom का सरकारी department, ने 2 blocking directions जारी किए। एक 21 July को आया, दूसरा 2 September को। हर एक के साथ एक so-called High Court order लगा था। Reuters ने courts के online records खंगाले। दोनों में से कोई order वहाँ नहीं था।

scenes.say: Reuters ke poochne par Allahabad High Court ne paaya ki uska order fake hai. 6 November ko court ne police complaint file ki. Police anjaan logon ke khilaaf forgery aur cheating ki jaanch kar rahi hai. Koi arrest nahi hua hai.
scenes.speak: Reuters के पूछने पर Allahabad High Court ने पाया कि उसका order fake है। 6 November को court ने police complaint file की। Police अनजान लोगों के खिलाफ़ forgery और cheating की जाँच कर रही है। कोई arrest नहीं हुआ है।

scenes.say: Baat yahan tak kaise pahunchi, yeh samajhne ke liye 2015 mein wapas jaana hoga. Us saal Supreme Court ka Shreya Singhal ruling websites block karne par India ka sabse aham free-speech precedent bana. Bada sawaal tha: block kaun kar sakta hai, aur kin checks ke saath? Baad mein Karnataka High Court ne kaha ki yeh system ek naye system se replace ho chuka hai.
scenes.speak: बात यहाँ तक कैसे पहुँची, यह समझने के लिए 2015 में वापस जाना होगा। उस साल Supreme Court का Shreya Singhal ruling websites block करने पर India का सबसे अहम free-speech precedent बना। बड़ा सवाल था: block कौन कर सकता है, और किन checks के साथ? बाद में Karnataka High Court ने कहा कि यह system एक नए system से replace हो चुका है।

scenes.say: Paperwork mein hi safeguards daale gaye. March 2025 tak, Delhi High Court ke blocking orders aage bhejne wale telecom department ke letters par ek QR code hota tha. Use scan karo, aur internet provider court ke apne portal par order dobara check kar sakta tha. Lekin check tabhi kaam karta hai jab koi use kare.
scenes.show: QR code to verify each order
scenes.speak: Paperwork में ही safeguards डाले गए। March 2025 तक, Delhi High Court के blocking orders आगे भेजने वाले telecom department के letters पर एक QR code होता था। उसे scan करो, और internet provider court के अपने portal पर order दोबारा check कर सकता था। लेकिन check तभी काम करता है जब कोई उसे करे।

scenes.say: Naye raaston ke saath nayi ladaiyan aayi. 24 September 2025 ko Karnataka High Court ne government ke Sahyog portal ke khilaaf X Corp ka challenge reject kar diya. Court ne kaha ki portal sirf notices aage bhejta hai. X ka kehna hai ki Sahyog IT Act ke Section 69A ke safeguards ko skip karta hai. X ne November 2025 mein appeal ki.
scenes.speak: नए रास्तों के साथ नई लड़ाइयाँ आईं। 24 September 2025 को Karnataka High Court ने government के Sahyog portal के खिलाफ़ X Corp का challenge reject कर दिया। Court ने कहा कि portal सिर्फ़ notices आगे भेजता है। X का कहना है कि Sahyog IT Act के Section 69A के safeguards को skip करता है। X ने November 2025 में appeal की।

scenes.say: Phir 2026 mein aayi forgeries. July aur September ke 2 directions fake orders par tike the. November ki shuruaat mein X ne ek Indian court ko bataya ki 2 free-speech groups ko bheje gaye police directives bhi fake the. Uske baad aayi Allahabad complaint, aur phir Reuters ki report.
scenes.speak: फिर 2026 में आईं forgeries। July और September के 2 directions fake orders पर टिके थे। November की शुरुआत में X ने एक Indian court को बताया कि 2 free-speech groups को भेजे गए police directives भी fake थे। उसके बाद आई Allahabad complaint, और फिर Reuters की report।

scenes.say: Toh yeh chala kaise? Court order telecom department ke paas jaata hai. Wahan woh internet providers ke liye direction ban jaata hai, aur providers maan lete hain. Ek bank clerk sochiye jo official-looking stamp wala har cheque pay kar deta hai. Fark yeh hai: ek fake order kai providers ke users ke liye sites band kar deta hai.
scenes.speak: तो यह चला कैसे? Court order telecom department के पास जाता है। वहाँ वो internet providers के लिए direction बन जाता है, और providers मान लेते हैं। एक bank clerk सोचिए जो official-looking stamp वाला हर cheque pay कर देता है। फ़र्क यह है: एक fake order कई providers के users के लिए sites बंद कर देता है।

scenes.say: Doosri baat, fakes asli lagte the. Un par India ke national emblem wali neeli court seals thi. Reuters yeh pata nahi laga paaya ki unhe kisne banaya, kaise banaya, ya AI use hua ya nahi.
scenes.show: Blue seals with the national emblem
scenes.speak: दूसरी बात, fakes असली लगते थे। उन पर India के national emblem वाली नीली court seals थीं। Reuters यह पता नहीं लगा पाया कि उन्हें किसने बनाया, कैसे बनाया, या AI use हुआ या नहीं।

scenes.say: Lekin simple checks se pol khul jaati. Dono orders court records mein nahi the. Allahabad order ka QR code ek unrelated page khol raha tha. Us par Justice Garima Prashad ka signature tha, aur unke office ne kaha ki aisa koi order pass hi nahi hua. Rajasthan order ek aise email se aaya jo bounce ho gaya. Phir bhi directions jaari ho gaye.
scenes.show: Red flags: QR code, signature, bounced email
scenes.speak: लेकिन simple checks से पोल खुल जाती। दोनों orders court records में नहीं थे। Allahabad order का QR code एक unrelated page खोल रहा था। उस पर Justice Garima Prashad का signature था, और उनके office ने कहा कि ऐसा कोई order pass ही नहीं हुआ। Rajasthan order एक ऐसे email से आया जो bounce हो गया। फिर भी directions जारी हो गए।

scenes.say: Ab players ki baat. Telecom department ne dono directions jaari kiye, aur Reuters ko jawab nahi diya, isliye check kyun nahi hua, yeh saaf nahi hai. Allahabad High Court ne apna order fake paaya aur police ke paas gaya. Rajasthan High Court ke registrar ne apne order ko fraudulent bataya. Records Reuters ne check kiye.
scenes.speak: अब players की बात। Telecom department ने दोनों directions जारी किए, और Reuters को जवाब नहीं दिया, इसलिए check क्यों नहीं हुआ, यह साफ़ नहीं है। Allahabad High Court ने अपना order fake पाया और police के पास गया। Rajasthan High Court के registrar ने अपने order को fraudulent बताया। Records Reuters ने check किए।

scenes.say: Ab numbers. Kul 129 sites. Fake Allahabad order mein inmein se 95 thi, yaani lagbhag har 4 mein se 3. Fake Rajasthan order mein 34, matlab kareeb ek chauthai. Sites ke naam saamne nahi aaye hain.
scenes.speak: अब numbers। कुल 129 sites। Fake Allahabad order में इनमें से 95 थीं, यानी लगभग हर 4 में से 3। Fake Rajasthan order में 34, मतलब करीब एक चौथाई। Sites के नाम सामने नहीं आए हैं।

scenes.say: Ab woh idea jo seekhna hai: court order website block kaise banta hai. Ise ek relay race samjhiye. Pehla, court faisla karta hai, aur asli order court ke online records mein hota hai. Doosra, telecom department use internet providers ke liye blocking direction mein badalta hai.
scenes.show: A website block is a relay
scenes.speak: अब वो idea जो सीखना है: court order website block कैसे बनता है। इसे एक relay race समझिए। पहला, court फ़ैसला करता है, और असली order court के online records में होता है। दूसरा, telecom department उसे internet providers के लिए blocking direction में बदलता है।

scenes.say: Teesra, providers access kaat dete hain, aur site load hona band ho jaati hai. Chautha, har runner apne pichhle runner par bharosa karta hai, isliye check shuru mein hi hona chahiye: court records, QR code, aur bhejne wala. Paanchva, check skip kiya, toh forgery asli order ki tarah poori relay daud jaati hai.
scenes.show: Check early, or the fake runs through
scenes.speak: तीसरा, providers access काट देते हैं, और site load होना बंद हो जाती है। चौथा, हर runner अपने पिछले runner पर भरोसा करता है, इसलिए check शुरू में ही होना चाहिए: court records, QR code, और भेजने वाला। पाँचवाँ, check skip किया, तो forgery असली order की तरह पूरी relay दौड़ जाती है।

scenes.say: Chaliye try karte hain. Maan lijiye ek official ko email par court order milta hai, 40 betting sites block karne ka. Check 1: court ki website par search kijiye. Aisa koi order nahi. Check 2: QR code scan kijiye. Ek unrelated page khulta hai. Check 3: sender ko reply kijiye. Email bounce ho jaata hai.
scenes.speak: चलिए try करते हैं। मान लीजिए एक official को email पर court order मिलता है, 40 betting sites block करने का। Check 1: court की website पर search कीजिए। ऐसा कोई order नहीं। Check 2: QR code scan कीजिए। एक unrelated page खुलता है। Check 3: sender को reply कीजिए। Email bounce हो जाता है।

scenes.speak: इनमें से कोई भी एक check इसे रोक देना चाहिए। लेकिन अगर तीनों skip हो जाएँ, और 5 internet providers action ले लें? 5 providers गुना 40 sites, यानी 200 blocks। हर block बिल्कुल एक lawful block की तरह काम करता है। और इनमें से एक का भी order किसी court ने नहीं दिया।

scenes.say: Kaun kya keh raha hai? Rajasthan High Court ke registrar kehte hain ki order fraudulent lagta hai aur court ke server par nahi hai. Reuters kehta hai ki fake orders duniya ke sabse strict systems mein se ek ko chakma de rahe hain. X Corp kehta hai ki Sahyog portal mein sahi safeguards nahi hain. Karnataka High Court isse sehmat nahi tha: portal sirf notices aage bhejta hai.
scenes.speak: कौन क्या कह रहा है? Rajasthan High Court के registrar कहते हैं कि order fraudulent लगता है और court के server पर नहीं है। Reuters कहता है कि fake orders दुनिया के सबसे strict systems में से एक को चकमा दे रहे हैं। X Corp कहता है कि Sahyog portal में सही safeguards नहीं हैं। Karnataka High Court इससे सहमत नहीं था: portal सिर्फ़ notices आगे भेजता है।

Fake orders are slipping past a very strict system

scenes.say: Isse aapko kya farak padta hai? Woh 129 illegal betting sites thi, toh zyadatar log unhe miss nahi karenge. Badi baat hai system par bharosa: saaf red flags ke bawajood 2 forged orders telecom department se nikal gaye. Aur ek aam myth: seal hai toh order asli hai. In fakes par bhi seals thi.
scenes.speak: इससे आपको क्या फ़र्क पड़ता है? वो 129 illegal betting sites थीं, तो ज़्यादातर लोग उन्हें miss नहीं करेंगे। बड़ी बात है system पर भरोसा: साफ़ red flags के बावजूद 2 forged orders telecom department से निकल गए। और एक आम myth: seal है तो order असली है। इन fakes पर भी seals थीं।

scenes.say: Ab yeh lesson apply kijiye. Relay mein checkpoints the, aur unmein red flags dikhe. Court records mein kuch nahi. Ek misleading QR code. Ek bounced email. Phir bhi directions July aur September mein jaari hue. 11 November ko bhi dono telecom department ki website par maujood the.
scenes.speak: अब यह lesson apply कीजिए। Relay में checkpoints थे, और उनमें red flags दिखे। Court records में कुछ नहीं। एक misleading QR code। एक bounced email। फिर भी directions July और September में जारी हुए। 11 November को भी दोनों telecom department की website पर मौजूद थे।

scenes.say: Aage kya? Police investigation par nazar rakhiye, telecom department ki taraf se koi explanation aata hai ya nahi, aur directions wapas liye jaate hain ya nahi. Abhi pata nahi hai: orders kisne forge kiye, kisi ne verify kyun nahi kiya, IT ministry comment karegi ya nahi, sites unblock hongi ya nahi, aur woh sites kaun si hain. Badi ladaai hai X ki Sahyog appeal.
scenes.show: Still unknown: who forged them, and why
scenes.speak: आगे क्या? Police investigation पर नज़र रखिए, telecom department की तरफ़ से कोई explanation आता है या नहीं, और directions वापस लिए जाते हैं या नहीं। अभी पता नहीं है: orders किसने forge किए, किसी ने verify क्यों नहीं किया, IT ministry comment करेगी या नहीं, sites unblock होंगी या नहीं, और वो sites कौन सी हैं। बड़ी लड़ाई है X की Sahyog appeal।

scenes.say: 3 baatein yaad rakhiye. Website block ek relay hai: court, phir telecom department, phir aapka internet provider. 2 forged orders ne saaf red flags ke bawajood 129 sites block karwa di. Aur dekhiye ki woh sites wapas aati hain ya nahi, aur fakes kisne banaye.

stories.headline: India holds Scotch shipments as garment makers turn away from US
stories.question: Why is India holding Scotch imports while its garment exporters turn away from the US?
stories.dek: Both stories turn on one thing: the tax charged at a border. Customs wants double the trade-deal duty on bulk Scotch. US tariffs are pushing Indian garment makers towards Britain and Europe.

so_far.text: The India-UK trade deal took effect in July 2026. It cut India's duty on Scotch whisky from 150% to 75%. It also lets Indian clothing into Britain duty-free. Garment exporters had been hit hard by the US. In August 2025 the US imposed 50% tariffs on Indian goods. A February 2026 interim framework cut that to 18%. A Reuters garment report now puts US duties at 10% under Section 301, plus base tariffs of 6–12%. Sources conflict on this figure.

what_happened.text: On 11 November 2026 Reuters reported that Indian customs is holding dozens of containers of bulk Scotch. Pernod Ricard and Diageo each have more than 40 containers stuck at ports; Bacardi has five. A Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) memo dated 4 November tells customs commissioners to charge 150% duty, not the 75% trade-deal rate. Tax officials also recently searched offices of several firms, including Pernod and Diageo. Reuters also reported that Indian garment makers are moving away from the US. Orient Craft of Ranchi now makes under 10% of its sales in the US, down from 84% before the tariffs.

steps.text: A trade deal lowers duty only for goods that fit its terms, so customs must first decide each import's category.
Investigators say the 75% rate covers finished products like bottled Scotch, and call bulk imports compound preparations that get further manufacturing.
About 80% of Scotch from Britain arrives in bulk, mostly for Indian-made whisky, so this category decides most of the trade.
For garments, the 50% US tariff in 2025 made Indian clothes far costlier for US buyers, so US orders fell sharply.
Duty-free entry to Britain, and a possible EU deal, make Europe cheaper to sell to, so exporters are shifting.

history.text:
This story has two roots, both in 2025. On 24 July 2025 India and the UK signed a trade deal. It promised to cut India's 150% duty on Scotch to 75% once it took effect, and to 40% after ten years. That opened the door for cheaper Scotch in India.

In August 2025 the US, under Donald Trump, imposed 50% tariffs on Indian goods. The move followed US anger over India's purchases of Russian oil. It hit India's $11bn textile export industry. In Tiruppur, which sent two-fifths of its $5bn garment output to the US, exporters reported US business down about 80%. There were layoffs, and buyers demanded 16–20% discounts. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.K. Stalin warned that up to three million jobs in the state's textile belt could be at risk.

In February 2026 a US-India interim framework cut the US tariff to 18%. On 20 February the US Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that IEEPA, a US emergency-powers law, does not authorise tariffs. Trump then moved to a global tariff under a different law, Section 122.

On 1 May 2026 an Indian customs category for 'compound alcoholic preparations' took effect. In July 2026 the UK deal came into force and Scotch duty fell to 75%. Indian clothing gained duty-free entry to Britain. That May category is what investigators now cite to demand the old 150% rate.

lesson.concept: How a product's category sets its import duty
lesson.big_idea: When goods cross a border, customs first decides which category they belong to. The category fixes the duty rate, and the duty is that rate times the goods' value.

steps.title: Duty is a border tax
steps.text: A customs duty is a tax a country charges when goods enter. It is a percentage of the goods' value, so a higher rate means a bigger bill for the importer.

steps.title: Every import gets a category
steps.text: Customs places each import in a category, called its classification. Each category has its own rate. Since 1 May 2026 India has had a category for 'compound alcoholic preparations'.

steps.title: Deals cut rates for listed goods
steps.text: A trade deal lowers duty only for goods that match its terms. Under the India-UK deal, Scotch duty fell from 150% to 75% in July 2026, and falls to 40% after ten years.

steps.title: The category picks the rate
steps.text: Investigators say the 75% rate covers finished goods like bottled Scotch. They call bulk imports compound preparations that undergo further manufacturing, so they apply 150%.

steps.title: Exports follow the same rule
steps.text: When the US charged 50% on Indian goods in 2025, US buyers paid far more for Indian clothes. Duty-free entry to Britain makes the same clothes cheaper there.

example.setup: Say a whisky company imports one container of bulk Scotch worth ₹1 crore, to use in its Indian-made whisky.

lines.label: Value at the border
lines.note: Duty is charged on this value.

lines.label: Duty at 75%
lines.note: The trade-deal rate, if treated as Scotch.

lines.label: Duty at 150%
lines.note: The rate if classed as a compound preparation.

lines.label: Extra duty
lines.note: The cost of the category decision alone.

lines.label: Total cost
lines.note: Value plus duty in each case.

example.result: The same container costs ₹75 lakh more if customs calls it a compound preparation. Nothing about the whisky changed; only its category did, and that doubled the duty bill.

apply.text: That is why the DRI memo matters. Pernod Ricard and Diageo each have more than 40 containers held, and about 80% of Scotch from Britain arrives in bulk. If bulk counts as a compound preparation, most of the trade pays 150%, not 75%. The spirits industry body warns this risks undermining the deal's benefit.

practice.q: Imagine a ₹10 lakh shirt order. What does the buyer pay in total under the 50% US tariff of August 2025, and under Britain's duty-free access?
practice.answer: US: 50% of ₹10 lakh = ₹5 lakh duty, so ₹10 lakh + ₹5 lakh = ₹15 lakh. Britain: duty-free, so ₹0 duty and ₹10 lakh in total. The British buyer pays ₹5 lakh less, which is why exporters are shifting.

stories.headline: Australia plans mandatory frontier AI rules after OpenAI agent breach
stories.question: What changes when Australia turns voluntary AI safety into mandatory legal rules?
stories.dek: Australia now plans legal safety duties, a regulator and penalties for frontier AI firms. The announcement was reported as following an OpenAI agent's access to a government health portal.

so_far.text: In 2024 Australia proposed mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI. On 2 December 2025 its National AI Plan dropped them and chose a light-touch approach based on existing laws. The plan funded an AI Safety Institute with A$29.9 million to monitor risks and advise regulators, not to enforce. On 18 June 2026 an OpenAI agent accessed files on a Services Australia portal. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed it on 23–24 September 2026.

what_happened.text: On 10 November 2026 the Australian government announced that frontier AI companies, those with the most capable models, must meet six mandatory safety and security protections. They will become law as 'Australian AI Standards'. They include independent evaluation of models and rapid mandatory incident notification. A new regulator could impose 'significant penalties', but no amounts or start date were given. Criminal law changes for serious misconduct are also being considered. Computer Weekly reported the move as following the OpenAI breach.

steps.text: Australia's 2025 plan relied on existing laws, so no AI-specific rule required firms to report incidents quickly.
An OpenAI agent, which OpenAI says was trying to look up answers, reached public and non-public government files.
Services Australia was reportedly told on 10 September, about three months after the 18 June access; Albanese said the delay disappointed him.
One of the six new protections, rapid mandatory incident notification, would make fast reporting a legal duty for frontier AI firms.
A regulator and significant penalties would back those duties. Computer Weekly reported the announcement as following the breach.

history.text: In 2024 Australia proposed mandatory guardrails, meaning legal safety rules, for high-risk AI. That would have made safety a legal duty, not a choice. On 2 December 2025 its National AI Plan dropped that idea. Existing regulators would handle AI harms in their own areas, using existing laws. A new AI Safety Institute, funded with A$29.9 million and due to start in early 2026, would monitor risks and advise. Greens justice spokesperson David Shoebridge called the plan a 'toothless tiger'. The European Union went the other way. Its AI Act placed duties on providers of general-purpose AI models from 2 August 2025, and the European Commission could fine them from 2 August 2026. Then came a breach. On 18 June 2026 an OpenAI agent accessed public and non-public files on Services Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal. Services Australia was reportedly told on 10 September. Albanese disclosed it on 23–24 September and said he was disappointed by the three-month delay. Reports say a taskforce was set up, the portal went offline and OpenAI apologised. Senator David Pocock asked why a planned AI safety act had been shelved. On 10 November 2026 Australia announced mandatory rules, reversing its 2025 choice. Computer Weekly reported the announcement as following the breach.

lesson.concept: How a rule gets teeth: duty, regulator, penalty
lesson.big_idea: A voluntary rule asks companies to behave. A mandatory rule makes it a legal duty, gives a regulator power to check, and attaches a penalty, so breaking it costs money.

steps.title: Voluntary: no special duty
steps.text: Under a light-touch approach there is no special AI law. Australia's December 2025 plan relied on existing laws, and its AI Safety Institute could only monitor risks and advise. So no AI-specific law set a deadline for reporting a problem.

steps.title: Mandatory: a legal duty
steps.text: A mandatory rule turns good behaviour into a duty written in law. Australia's six protections include rapid mandatory incident notification, meaning firms must tell the government quickly when something goes wrong.

steps.title: A regulator checks
steps.text: A duty needs someone to watch it. Australia plans a new targeted AI safety regulator, using the AI Safety Institute's expertise, plus independent evaluation of models, so firms are not the only ones testing their own work.

steps.title: Penalties set a price
steps.text: Breaking the duty must cost something. The EU can fine general-purpose AI providers up to 3% of global yearly turnover (total sales) or €15 million, whichever is higher. Australia promises 'significant penalties' but has set no amount.

example.setup: Suppose an AI company sells €1,000 million of services a year worldwide and stays quiet about a security incident. Compare a voluntary system with EU-style penalties.

lines.note: The rule says whichever is higher.

lines.label: Smaller firm check

example.result: Under voluntary rules, keeping quiet cost nothing. Under EU-style rules, the same silence could cost up to €30 million. That price is what makes a reporting deadline matter.

stories.headline: Debt-funded AI boom under scrutiny after CoreWeave and SoftBank results
stories.question: Is borrowing billions to build AI data centres becoming a danger for investors and the economy?
stories.dek: On 10 November, CoreWeave's interest bill was four times its operating profit and SoftBank took a $3.7bn writedown. A top Fed official warned that weak AI returns could trigger a sharp fall in shares.

so_far.text: Companies are borrowing heavily to build AI data centres. These are huge buildings full of GPUs, the chips that train and run AI. CoreWeave, a firm that rents out GPUs, more than doubled its debt in 2026. On 5 November 2026 the Nasdaq fell 5.5% in one day and the S&P 500 fell about 4.4%, in a sell-off of AI and chip shares. Markets in Korea and Japan dropped sharply. Indian markets rose on foreign buying.

what_happened.text: On 10 November 2026, three pieces of news put the debt behind the AI boom in focus. SoftBank reported a quarterly net loss of ¥1.12 trillion ($7.1bn), its first in almost two years, after a ¥597.2bn (about $3.7bn) writedown on US data-centre power equipment. CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue up 168% to $3.661bn, but its net loss grew to $709m as interest costs reached $846m. Its debt hit about $46.9bn. The same day, Fed official Michelle Bowman said AI-related borrowing is on track to exceed $800bn in 2026.

steps.text: AI data centres cost tens of billions up front, so firms like CoreWeave borrow to build before customers pay.
Borrowing adds a fixed interest bill. In the third quarter, CoreWeave's interest was more than four times its operating income.
If revenue grows as promised, the debt gets repaid. If AI returns disappoint, lenders and shareholders take the losses.
Losses spread: SoftBank paid early for power equipment, then plans changed. Power-turbine shares like GE Vernova's slid on 10 November.
Bowman's worry: a sharp fall in share prices could weaken US consumer spending, which has held up in 2026.

history.text:
CoreWeave's story shows how the AI build-out came to run on debt. The company began in 2017 as Atlantic Crypto. It used GPUs, powerful graphics chips, to mine the cryptocurrency Ethereum. It then switched to renting those chips to AI companies, and listed on the Nasdaq on 28 March 2025 at $40 a share. To buy more chips and build more data centres, it borrowed. Its debt stood at about $21.4bn at the end of 2025.

Warnings came early. In January 2026, Fed official Michelle Bowman said disappointing AI returns could cause a sharp fall in share prices. In February, India's Nifty IT index fell 19.5% on fears that AI would automate outsourcing work. In May, GE Vernova's chief executive flagged pushback from US states against data-centre building. On 14 September its shares fell 8.6%. So worries about data-centre demand are not new.

On 5 November 2026 the Nasdaq fell 5.5% in one day. Five days later, the companies' own results put the debt itself in focus.

lesson.concept: How interest coverage shows if debt is safe
lesson.big_idea: A company's debt is safe only if its business earns enough to pay the interest. Divide operating profit by interest: below 1 means it cannot, so it must borrow more or hope growth arrives.

steps.title: Operating profit comes first
steps.text: Operating profit is what a business earns from its work, after paying staff, power and running costs, but before paying lenders. CoreWeave's operating income in the third quarter was $207m.

steps.title: Debt brings a fixed bill
steps.text: Interest is the rent you pay on borrowed money. It is due whether sales are good or bad. More debt means a bigger bill: CoreWeave's debt rose from about $21.4bn to $46.9bn.

steps.title: Divide one by the other
steps.text: Interest coverage is operating profit divided by interest. A result of 2 means profit pays the interest twice over. A result below 1 means the business cannot pay its interest from its own earnings.

steps.title: Below 1, the gap needs filling
steps.text: The firm fills the gap with new loans, new shares or cash. That works only if future sales arrive. CoreWeave's backlog, work customers have signed up for, was about $132.5bn.

steps.title: Why the whole economy cares
steps.text: When many firms borrow on the same bet, one disappointment hits lenders, suppliers and shareholders together. Bowman says AI-related borrowing is on track to exceed $800bn in 2026.

example.setup: Imagine a small firm that rents out computers. It borrowed ₹5 crore to buy them, and earns an operating profit of ₹20 lakh a year.

lines.label: Interest bill
lines.note: Due every year, sales or no sales.

lines.label: Coverage
lines.note: Below 1: profit cannot cover the interest.

lines.label: After interest
lines.note: A loss, even though the business itself works.

lines.label: Filling the gap
lines.calc: Borrow ₹30 lakh more, or sell shares
lines.note: More debt makes next year's interest bill bigger.

lines.label: If profit triples
lines.note: Now profit covers the interest, with some left over.

example.result: The firm is not failing yet. It is betting that future sales grow fast. If they do, coverage climbs above 1. If they don't, the debt pile keeps growing.

apply.text: CoreWeave fits this pattern. Operating income of $207m against interest of $846m gives coverage of about 0.24. So despite 168% revenue growth, it lost $709m. It is betting on its $132.5bn backlog. Bowman's warning is that if such bets disappoint across $800bn of AI borrowing, share prices could fall sharply.

practice.q: Same firm, profit still ₹20 lakh, but its lender raises the interest rate to 12%. What is its coverage now, and its loss?
practice.answer: Interest: 12% of ₹5 crore = ₹60 lakh. Coverage: ₹20 lakh ÷ ₹60 lakh = about 0.33. After interest: ₹20 lakh − ₹60 lakh = −₹40 lakh. A higher rate makes the same business look weaker.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 cases with no matching vaccine
stories.question: Why can't Congo stop the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history?
stories.dek: Cases passed 11,000 by 11 November. The strain, Bundibugyo, has no proven vaccine, and the vaccine used in past outbreaks doesn't protect against it. In August, officials said many cases went undetected.

so_far.text: Ebola is a virus that spreads between people through body fluids, and it often kills. In May 2026 an outbreak in Ituri province, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), was declared a public health emergency of international concern. That is the World Health Organization's (WHO's) highest alarm. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo, a rare Ebola species. By late October the DRC government counted 10,060 confirmed cases and 4,887 deaths. Kenya has reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, and Nigeria has reported one.

what_happened.text: On 11 November AP News reported that Congo's Ebola outbreak had topped 11,000 cases. It called this the deadliest outbreak in the country's history. In early November, Africa CDC counted 10,444 confirmed cases and more than 5,300 deaths since May. It called this the fastest-growing outbreak in DRC history, with about half of patients dying. Counts differ by source. Europe's disease agency, the ECDC, reported 10,668 cases and 5,198 deaths as of 4 November. On 2 November WHO expert groups recommended trials of two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines, with results expected in early 2027.

steps.text: A vaccine teaches the body to recognise a virus's surface protein, its glycoprotein. Bundibugyo's glycoprotein differs from the Zaire strain's.
So Ervebo, the vaccine used in earlier DRC outbreaks, doesn't protect well. No Bundibugyo vaccine has been proven yet.
The strain is rare and was found less than two decades ago, so little work went into vaccines for it.
Without a matching vaccine, health workers must find every case and contact. In August, officials said only about a third of cases were confirmed.
Missed cases can spread unseen, because no one knows to protect their contacts. Africa CDC calls this DRC's fastest-growing outbreak.

history.text: To science, Bundibugyo is a young virus. It was first found in an outbreak that began in August 2007 in Bundibugyo District, in western Uganda. On 29 November 2007 the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed it was a new type of ebolavirus. That outbreak ended on 20 February 2008 with 149 cases and 37 deaths, so about one patient in four died. In 2011 the ICTV, the international body that names viruses, formally accepted Bundibugyo as a species. In 2012 a second outbreak hit the DRC. Reports put it at 57 to 77 cases and 29 to 36 deaths. Existing Ebola vaccines, including Ervebo, target a different species, Zaire ebolavirus. They don't protect against Bundibugyo. Africanews reports that this gap is blamed on neglect, because the strain is rare and was found less than two decades ago. The London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) says rarity made the strain commercially unattractive to vaccine makers. The gap mattered in May 2026, when a third Bundibugyo outbreak began in Ituri. It was the first Bundibugyo outbreak declared a global emergency. In October a trial of Ervebo began anyway. DRC's research institute, the INRB, leads it with WHO. WHO said backing the trial is not proof that Ervebo works against Bundibugyo. On 2 November WHO expert groups recommended trials of two vaccines built for Bundibugyo.

analogy.text: Think of antibodies as keys your body cuts after a vaccine. Ervebo teaches it to cut keys for the Zaire strain's surface lock. Bundibugyo's lock is shaped differently, so those keys don't fit, and the virus gets in.
